hpi_details: 2-week history of recurrent, abrupt-onset dizzy spells, lightheadedness, and feeling on the verge of blacking out when walking or rising from a chair. clinical_knowledge.topic: Second-Degree AV Block, Mobitz Type II evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Second-Degree AV Block, Mobitz Type II is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes urgent hospital admission with continuous cardiac monitoring and bed rest with bathroom privileges only (high risk of unpredictable progression to complete third-degree AV block or ventricular standstill), adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: frequent dizzy spells, near fainting, and heart dropping beats over 2 weeks

Key HPI features: 2-week history of recurrent, abrupt-onset dizzy spells, lightheadedness, and feeling on the verge of blacking out when walking or rising from a chair. Reports sensation of his pulse becoming exceptionally slow or dropping several beats in a row. Experienced two episodes of near-syncope where he had to grab a table to avoid falling. Denies chest pain, shortness of breath, or seizure activity. Had a pacemaker discussion years ago but never followed up.

Objective/Exam findings: Examine pulse: slow, irregular pulse at 42 bpm with intermittent dropped beats. Vitals: BP 115/68 mmHg. 12-lead ECG: normal constant PR interval on conducted beats, but sudden unexpected non-conducted P waves (dropped QRS complexes) occurring in a 2:1 or 3:2 conduction ratio with normal sinus P-P intervals (Second-Degree Atrioventricular Block - Mobitz Type II). Check QRS duration (often widened indicating infranodal His-Purkinje conduction disease). Bloods: U&Es (rule out hyperkalaemia), troponin, digoxin level if applicable.
Relevant background/PMH: hypertension, chronic kidney disease stage 3, osteoarthritis
Current medications: amlodipine 5mg OD, paracetamol PRN (not taking beta-blockers or rate-slowing drugs)
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Second-Degree AV Block, Mobitz Type II.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Sick sinus syndrome without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Syncope without warning — high risk of progression to complete heart block.
management_principles: Urgent hospital admission with continuous cardiac monitoring and bed rest with bathroom privileges only (high risk of unpredictable progression to complete third-degree AV block or ventricular standstill)

If severe symptomatic bradycardia or haemodynamic instability occurs: administer IV atropine (though less reliable in infranodal Mobitz II) or IV isoprenaline, and prepare transcutaneous/transvenous temporary pacing
Urgent cardiology consult for permanent dual-chamber pacemaker (PPM) implantation
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

source_refs.title: 2018 ACC/AHA/HRS Guideline on the Evaluation and Management of Patients With Bradycardia and Cardiac Conduction Delay

reference_soap.subjective:
Chief Complaint: frequent dizzy spells, near fainting, and heart dropping beats over 2 weeks

2-week history of recurrent, abrupt-onset dizzy spells, lightheadedness, and feeling on the verge of blacking out when walking or rising from a chair. Reports sensation of his pulse becoming exceptionally slow or dropping several beats in a row. Experienced two episodes of near-syncope where he had to grab a table to avoid falling. Denies chest pain, shortness of breath, or seizure activity. Had a pacemaker discussion years ago but never followed up.
reference_soap.objective: Examine pulse: slow, irregular pulse at 42 bpm with intermittent dropped beats. Vitals: BP 115/68 mmHg. 12-lead ECG: normal constant PR interval on conducted beats, but sudden unexpected non-conducted P waves (dropped QRS complexes) occurring in a 2:1 or 3:2 conduction ratio with normal sinus P-P intervals (Second-Degree Atrioventricular Block - Mobitz Type II). Check QRS duration (often widened indicating infranodal His-Purkinje conduction disease). Bloods: U&Es (rule out hyperkalaemia), troponin, digoxin level if applicable.
reference_soap.assessment: Second-Degree Atrioventricular Block (Mobitz Type II) causing symptomatic bradycardia and presyncope. DDx: Mobitz Type I (Wenckebach - progressive PR prolongation before dropped beat; benign nodal disease), Complete (Third-Degree) AV Block, Sick Sinus Syndrome, drug-induced bradycardia.
reference_soap.plan: Urgent hospital admission with continuous cardiac monitoring and bed rest with bathroom privileges only (high risk of unpredictable progression to complete third-degree AV block or ventricular standstill). If severe symptomatic bradycardia or haemodynamic instability occurs: administer IV atropine (though less reliable in infranodal Mobitz II) or IV isoprenaline, and prepare transcutaneous/transvenous temporary pacing. Urgent cardiology consult for permanent dual-chamber pacemaker (PPM) implantation.

learning_objectives: Differentiate Mobitz Type II AV block (constant PR interval before suddenly dropped QRS; high risk infranodal block) from Mobitz Type I Wenckebach (progressive PR prolongation)
Recognise the high clinical danger of Mobitz Type II progressing unpredictably to complete heart block or asystole
Outline the emergency step-up bradycardia management protocol from pharmacological adjuncts to temporary and permanent pacing
Counsel elderly patients clearly regarding permanent pacemaker implantation procedure, safety, and lifestyle benefits

teaching.diagnosis: Second-Degree AV Block, Mobitz Type II
teaching.one_liner: Conduction to the ventricles fails intermittently and unpredictably. It progresses to complete block, so it needs a pacemaker.
red_flags: Syncope without warning — high risk of progression to complete heart block

must_ask.say: Do you get any warning at all, or does it come out of nowhere?
How often is this happening, and is it getting more frequent?
Are you on any heart tablets — beta blockers, digoxin, or similar?
Have you actually lost consciousness, or only come close?
Have you hurt yourself when this happened?
Have you been unusually tired or short of breath?

history.answer: I have been having these sudden dizzy spells for the past two weeks, and twice I felt like I was right on the verge of blacking out.
It is not a spinning room feeling at all; it is a sudden lightheadedness where I feel faint, like the power is suddenly cut from my head.
It started about two weeks ago out of the blue, and the spells have been happening several times a day.
Each dizzy spell lasts only a few seconds, but in that moment I feel like I am about to lose consciousness.
It often hits when I stand up from an armchair or start walking, but sometimes it happens when I am just sitting still.
No, they come on very abruptly without any warning, just a sudden heavy thump or pause in my chest and instant lightheadedness.
I have not fully passed out yet, but twice I came so close that I had to grab a table to stop myself from dropping to the floor.
Yes, right when the dizziness hits, I feel like my heart slows down to a crawl or drops several beats in a row.
No, I have not had any chest pain, tightness, or pressure.
No, I have not had any shortness of breath while resting or during the spells.
No, I have not felt nauseated, and I have not vomited.
No ringing in my ears, no clogged sensation, and my hearing has not changed at all.
No, I have not had double vision, slurred speech, facial numbness, or any weakness in my arms or legs.
No, I have not had any new severe headache, and my neck is not stiff or painful.
No, I have had no fever, chills, cough, or any recent viral cold.
No black or bloody bowel movements, no vomiting or diarrhea, and I have been drinking plenty of water.
I do not have diabetes, and I eat my three meals regularly each day without skipping.
No, I have never had migraines, and lights or sounds do not bother me when I am dizzy.
No, I am not having panic attacks or rapid breathing, although these dizzy blackouts do make me nervous.
I managed to catch myself on furniture both times, so fortunately I have not fallen or sustained any injuries.
I have felt somewhat more tired and drained over the past two weeks, but nothing stops me except these sudden dizzy spells.
I think the electrical wiring in my heart is simply fraying and wearing out because of my old age.
I live alone, and my biggest fear is having a sudden blackout, falling hard, and breaking my hip.
A doctor told me years ago that I might eventually need a pacemaker for my heart, but I never went back to follow up on it.
I have high blood pressure, stage three chronic kidney disease, and osteoarthritis in my knees and hands.
I had an appendectomy when I was a young man, but I have not had any other surgeries or hospitalizations.
I take amlodipine five milligrams once daily for my blood pressure and occasional paracetamol for arthritis; I do not take beta-blockers or any other heart drugs.
I do not have any known allergies to medicines, foods, or anything else.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used tobacco products in my life.
I only drink a small glass of wine on rare special occasions, maybe three or four times a year.
I am a retired farmer living alone at home, and I wear an emergency alert pendant around my neck just in case.
My father died of a stroke in his eighties and my mother had arthritis, but there is no family history of sudden cardiac death or early heart disease.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 115/68 mmHg, heart rate 42 beats per minute with intermittent dropped beats, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, temperature 36.7 C, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air.
Lying blood pressure 115/68 mmHg with heart rate 42 bpm; standing blood pressure 112/66 mmHg with heart rate 42 bpm, showing no significant orthostatic drop.
No spontaneous, gaze-evoked, or positional nystagmus; Dix-Hallpike test and head impulse test are normal and do not elicit vertigo.
Cranial nerves II through XII are grossly intact with normal visual fields, extraocular movements, facial symmetry, and palate elevation.
Finger-to-nose and rapid alternating movements are normal; Romberg test is negative, and tandem gait is intact without ataxia.
Marked bradycardia at 42 beats per minute with sudden intermittent pauses; normal S1 and S2 with no murmurs, gallops, or rubs.
Radial, brachial, and carotid pulses are slow at 42 beats per minute with intermittent dropped beats, but symmetric and full.
Lungs are clear to auscultation bilaterally with normal vesicular breath sounds and no wheezes or crackles.
No peripheral edema or signs of venous stasis in either lower extremity.
